This is claim petition filed by petitioner Ms.Neha who suffered injuries in an accident.

As per the the claimant on 16.11.2016 when injured/petitioner was going by an auto rickshaw no.UP 14FT 0225 MACT No.334/2017 Page 1 from her home to Ghaziabad, at about 11.00 a.m. when the petitioner reached near Bansla Nehar (canal) Loni, offending truck bearing registration no.DL 1M 6554 being driven by respondent no.1 in a rash and negligent manner, without following the traffic rules hit the above auto rickshaw from opposite direction and thereby rickshaw fell on the road and petitioner sustained grievous injuries.
After the accident claimant was brought to Sarvodaya Hospital Ghaziabad where she was given treatment till 14.12.2016.
However on account of serious condition of injuries sustained by injured she was taken to Sir Ganga Ram Hospital, New Delhi for further treatment.

It is the settled proposition of law that an action founded on the principle of fault liability, the proof of rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle is sine qua non.
However, the standard of proof is not as strict as applied in criminal cases and evidence is to be tested on the touchstone of preponderance of probabilities.
Holistic view is to be taken while dealing with the Claim Petition based upon negligence.
Strict rules of evidence are not applicable in an inquiry conducted by the Claims Tribunal.

sentences.text: In the facts of the present case petitioner/PW1 in her deposition has specifically deposed that she took an auto rickshaw no.UP MACT No.334/2017 Page 4 14FT 0225 from her home for going to Ghaziabad and when her auto rickshaw reached near Banthala Canal, Loni, offending truck bearing no.DL 1M 6554 was being driven by its driver in a very high speed, rashly and negligently and without taking any caution hit the auto rickshaw from opposite and wrong direction and due to that accident she sustained grievous accidental injuries.
PW1 says that accident happened only due to negligent driving of driver of offending vehicle no.DL 1M 6554.

PW1 says that crime no.1474/16 was registered at PS Loni against driver of offending truck no.DL 1M 6554.
12.
PW1 was duly cross examined.

No doubt in cross- examination PW1 stated that she do not know the number of offending vehicle, however this Tribunal finds that deposition of PW1 regarding the manner in which accident took place has been very consistent.

It is quite possible that injured in an accident having undergone long treatment,
may not be able to recollect registration number of offending truck.
PW1 in cross-examination stated that there was a divider in between the road and the offending truck which was coming from the side of Ghaziabad, came on the wrong side of the road.
PW1 says that the speed of auto rickshaw was at very normal speed.

It is settled law that in case of head-on collusion, in every such case,
contributory negligence cannot be assumed, if there is no evidence to prove it.

13. As such this Tribunal finds that evidence of PW1 has been substantively consistent and cogent proving that accident took place only on account of rash and negligent driving of truck no.DL 1M 6554 as it came on the wrong side of the road and was being driven in a high speed.

Above said fact Neha vs Anil Kumar on 17 November, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/126686646/

Site plan also proves that truck went on the wrong side of the road while coming from Ghaziabad and going towards village Banthala, Loni and struck the auto rickshaw, which claimant was occupying, from the front.

Issue No.2 14.
The scope of compensation in injury cases has been considered by Hon'ble Supreme Court in case titled as Mr. R.D. Hattangadi v. M/s Pest Control (India) Pvt. Ltd., 1995 AIR 755.

entities.text: R.D. Hattangadi v. M/s Pest Control (India) Pvt. Ltd., 1995 AIR 755
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
The relevant extract is as under:
"Broadly speaking while fixing an amount of compensation payable to a victim of an accident, the damages have to be assessed separately as pecuniary damages and special damages.

Pecuniary damages are those which the victim has actually incurred and which is capable of being calculated in terms of money-, whereas non-pecuniary damages are those which are incapable of being assessed by arithmetical calculations.

In order to appreciate two concepts pecuniary damages may, include expenses incurred by the claimant: (i) medical attendance; (ii) loss of earning of profit upto the date of trial; (iii) other material loss.
So far non- pecuniary damages are concerned

,
they may include (i) damages for mental and physical shock, pain suffering, already suffered or likely to be suffered in future; (ii) damages to compensate for the loss of amenities of life which may include a variety of matters i.e. on account of injury the claimant may not be able to walk, run or sit;
(iii) damages for the loss of expectation of life, i.e. on account of injury the normal longevity of the person concerned is shortened; (iv) inconvenience, discomfort,
disappointment, hardship, frustration and MACT No.334/2017 Page 6 mental stress in life."
15. Further, in Raj Kumar v. Ajay Kumar & another (2011) 1 SCC 343, Hon'ble Supreme Court of India laid down general principles for computation of compensation in injury cases.

sentences.text:
The relevant paras of the judgment are reproduced as under:
4.

The provisions of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 ("the Act", for short) makes it clear that the award must be just, which means that compensation should, to the extent possible, fully and adequately restore the claimant to the position prior to the accident.
The object of awarding damages is to make good the loss suffered as a result of wrong done as far as money can do so, in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner.

The court or the Tribunal shall have to assess the damages objectively and exclude from consideration any speculation or fancy, though some conjecture with reference to the nature of disability and its consequences, is inevitable.

A person is not only to Neha vs Anil Kumar on 17 November, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/126686646/
4 be compensated for the physical injury, but also for the loss which he suffered as a result of such injury.

This means that he is to be compensated for his inability to lead a full life, his inability to enjoy those normal amenities which he would have enjoyed but for the injuries, and his inability to earn as much as he used to earn or could have earned.

5. The heads under which compensation is awarded in personal injury cases are the following:
Pecuniary Damages (special damages)

(i) Expenses relating to treatment, hospitalization, medicines, transportation,
nourishing food and miscellaneous expenditure.

(ii) Loss of earnings (and other gains) which the injured would have made had he not been injured, comprising:
(a) Loss of earning during the period of treatment.
(b) Loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability.
MACT No.334/2017 Page 7  (iii) Future medical expenses.
 Non-Pecuniary Damages (general damages)
 (iv) Damages to pain, suffering and trauma as a  consequence of the injuries.

(v) Loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects  of marriage)
 (vi) Loss of expectation of life (shortening of  normal longevity).

In routine personal injury cases, compensation will be awarded only under heads (i),
(ii), (a) and (iv).

It is only in serious cases of injury, where there is specific medical evidence corroborating the evidence of the claimant, that compensation will be granted under any of the heads (ii), (b), (iii), (v) and (vi) relating to loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability, future medical expenses, loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage) and loss of expectation of life.
16.

In the light of the aforementioned judgments, the compensation to which the petitioner is entitled shall be as under:-
PECUNIARY DAMAGES :

Medical Expenses:

17. PW1 in her evidence has stated that immediately after the accident she was brought to Sarvodaya Hospital Ghaziabad where she was treated uptill 14.12.2016, however on account of her serious condition she was brought to Sir Ganga Ram Hospital Delhi for better treatment.
PW1 state that she received grievous injuries all over her body and received serious right foot injury and head injury in that accident.
PW1 further deposes that her right foot injury was so grievous and serious that she was operated upon and her right foot was amputated below the knee.
She became permanently disabled due to injuries suffered in the accident.
MACT No.334/2017 Page 8 18.
PW1 says that she remained admitted in Sir Ganga Ram Hospital on three times, firstly from 14.12.2016 to 06.01.2017 secondly from 27.01.2017 to 27.01.2017 and thirdly from 05.05.2017 to 09.05.2017.
PW1 says that she had incurred about Rs.10 lakhs on her treatment, out of which she got benefit of health insurance/mediclaim of Rs.5 lakhs, however rest of the amount was paid by her.
PW1 has proved in her evidence medical bills, treatment record which are Ex.PW1/1 to Ex.PW1/4 which include details of artificial limb bill and repair charges.
19. Regarding the medical expenditure petitioner also examined PW3 Dr.Shubham Bhardwaj who proved the bill and receipt of artificial limb Ex.PW3/B.

PW4 is Gaurav Malhotra from Sir Ganga Ram hospital who also proved details of admission/discharge of claimant from said hospital and proved the attested copy of medical record Ex.PW4/1.
20.

Having considered the evidence as noted above, from the deposition of PW1 coupled with the bills proved in her evidence as well as list of same Ex.PW1/1 it is proved that there are bills of Sarvodaya Hospital and thereafter there are also bills of total amount of Rs.6,18,091/- from Sir Ganga Ram Hospital, out of which Rs.5,24,853/- was reimbursed from mediclaim insurance (Max Bupa Health Insurance) as reflected from final bill raised in Sir Ganga Ram Hospital.
Beside this there is also evidence of OPD receipts, medical/pharmacy bills of total amount of Rs.7,561/-.

As such there is total of medical expenses of all the hospitals, treatment expenses of amount of Rs.4,11,550/-.
21.

It has come on the record from discharge summary of Sir Ganga Ram Hospital as well as from the medical record of Sarvodaya Hospital that claimant received grievous injuries all over her body and had locomotor disability on her right leg.

Her medical condition was assessed MACT No.334/2017 Page 9 by medical board of GTB Hospital, and assessed that claimant was suffering from permanent disability to the extent of 60% in relation to right lower limb which is proved in the evidence of PW2.
22.

Beside above mentioned medical expenses, from the evidence of PW1 and documents Ex.PW1/4 which is also established from evidence of PW3 and documents Ex.PW3/B, it is proved that claimant also incurred expenses for fitment of TT prosthesis with C Walk Foot (artificial limb) and incurred expenditure of Rs.66,000/- vide invoice date 20.03.2018, Rs.3,45,000/- vide invoice dated Neha vs Anil Kumar on 17 November, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/126686646/
6 22.06.2017, Rs.25,700/- vide invoice dated 24.10.2019, Rs.1,50,000/- vide invoice dated 30.05.2017, Rs.16,000/- vide invoice dated 12.03.2018.

As such total expenses were Rs.6,02,700/-.
23.
Thus, total medical expenses incurred by claimant on account of her medical expenditure comes to be Rs.10,14,250/- (Rs.4,11,550 + Rs.6,02,700).
Loss of earning during treatment:
24. PW1 injured Neha in her affidavit has testified that she was working as Intern Dentist under a dentist Dr.Prashant Sharma at Ghaziabad and was earning Rs.12,000/- per month.

Petitioner in her evidence has proved one document Ex.PW1/6 i.e. certification of Dr.Prashant Sharma, BDS mentioning that petitioner Neha was working as intern in his clinic and was drawing salary of Rs.12,000/- per month.
Beside this petitioner also proved documents i.e. certificate of intermediate examination, fourth semester of BDS in Chaudhary Charan Singh University Meerut which are Ex.PW1/7 and Ex.PW1/8 (colly.).

Above mentioned documents coupled with the testimony of PW1,
is sufficient to prove that petitioner was working as intern with a dentist being a student of BDS and was drawing Rs.12,000/- per month.
MACT No.334/2017 Page 10 25
. PW1 petitioner Neha in her affidavit of evidence has testified that after the accident on 13.12.2016 she was taken to Sarvodaya Hospital, till 14.12.2016.

Thereafter on account of her serious condition, for better treatment she was taken to Sir Ganga Ram Hospital where she remained hospitalized from 14.12.2016 to 06.01.2017, thereafter remained hospitalized on 27.01.2017 and later from 05.05.2017 to 09.05.2017.
Relevant discharge summary are on the record as Ex.PW1/3.
Thus, perusal of the evidence of PW1 and documents proved, petitioner remained under treatment from 13.12.2016 to 09.05.2017.
Although it is stated that petitioner is still taking the treatment but as per the medical documents petitioner lastly discharged from Sir Ganga Ram hospital on 09.05.2017.
Beside this it came on the record from the evidence of PW3 that petitioner had artificial limb, the payment of which has been proved by bill Ex.PW3/B.
Thus, on holistic assessment of evidence, documents on the record, this Tribunal finds that petitioner lost earning for treatment for five months.

As such this Tribunal finds that petitioner is entitled for sum of Rs.60,000/-
(Rs.12,000 X 5) on account of loss of earning during treatment.

Loss of future earning due to disability :
26.

In case of Raj Kumar v. Ajay Kumar & Anr. (2011) 1 SCC 343, Hon'ble Supreme Court of India determined the broad criteria for assessment of permanent disability for ascertaining the purpose of future loss of earning and also laid down step by step procedure for assessment of disability and for ascertainment to the effect of the permanent disability on the actual earning capacity.

sentences.text:
Relevant paras of the judgment are reproduced as under:-
Neha vs Anil Kumar on 17 November, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/126686646/
7 "9.
Therefore, the Tribunal has to first decide MACT No.334/2017 Page 11 whether there is any permanent disability and if so, the extent of such permanent disability.

This means that the tribunal should consider and decide with reference to the evidence:
 (i) Whether the disablement is permanent or  temporary;
 (ii) If the disablement is permanent, whether it is permanent total disablement or permanent partial disablement;
(iii) If the disablement percentage is expressed with reference to any specific limb,
then the effect of such disablement of the limb on the functioning of the entire body,
that is the permanent disability suffered by the person.
If the Tribunal concludes that there is no permanent disability then there is no question of proceeding further and determining the loss of future earning capacity.
But if the Tribunal concludes that there is permanent disability then it will proceed to ascertain its extent.

After the Tribunal ascertains the actual extent of permanent disability of the claimant based on the medical evidence, it has to determine whether such permanent disability has affected or will affect his earning capacity.
10. Ascertainment of the effect of the permanent disability on the actual earning capacity involves three steps.

The tribunal has to first ascertain what activities of the claimant could carry on in spite of the permanent disability and what he could not do as a result of permanent disability (this is also relevant for awarding compensation under the head of loss of amenities of life).
The second step is to ascertain his avocation, profession and nature of work before the accident, as also his age.

The third step is to find out whether (i) the claimant is totally disabled from earning any kind of livelihood or (ii) whether in spite of the permanent disability, the claimant could still effectively carry on the activities and functions, which he was earlier carrying on, or (iii) Whether he was prevented or restricted from discharging his previous activities and functions so that he continues to earn or MACT No.334/2017 Page 12 can continue to earn his livelihood."
....If doctor has given evidence about percentage of permanent disability, Tribunal will have to seek doctors opinion as to whether it is possible to deduce the corresponding functional permanent disability with reference to whole body and if so to what percentage.

13. We may now summarize the principles discussed above:
(i). All injuries (or permanent disabilities arising from injuries), do not result in loss of earning capacity.
(ii).
The percentage of permanent disability with reference to the whole body of a person, cannot be assumed to be the percentage of loss of earning capacity.

To put it differently, the percentage of loss of earning capacity is not the same as the Neha vs Anil Kumar on 17 November, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/126686646/
8 percentage of permanent disability (except in a few cases, where the Tribunal on the basis of evidence, concludes that percentage of loss of earning capacity is the same as percentage of permanent disability).
(iii).
The doctor who treated an injured- claimant or who examined him subsequently to assess the extent of his permanent disability can give evidence only in regard the extent of permanent disability.
The loss of earning capacity is something that will have to be assessed by the Tribunal with reference to the evidence in entirety.

(iv). The same permanent disability may result in different percentages of loss of earning capacity in different persons, depending upon the nature of profession,
occupation or job, age, education and other factors."
27. Keeping in view the ratio as discussed above, in the present case it is evident on record that as a result of the injuries sustained by petitioner MACT No.334/2017 Page 13 in an accident, she suffered 60% of permanent disability in relation to right lower limb.
It came in the deposition of PW1 as well as other medical documents proved on the record that petitioner's right foot was operated and amputated below the knee.
Artificial limb has been implanted later.

In the evidence of PW2 Dr.V.K.
Goel who proved the disability certificate Ex.PW2/A the 60% of medical permanent disability is on account of loco motor disability.
28. Now question arises how much 60% of the permanent medical disability has effected on the functional ability of petitioner.
As noted above petitioner was working as an intern with a dentist being a student of BDS.
In cross-examination of PW2 it came that amputation was 8cm from the knee joint line and therefore medical permanent disability has been ascertained to be 60%.
PW2 has testified that he cannot assess the disability of the patient in relation to whole body.
From the evidence of PW3 Dr.Shubham Bhardwaj who proved the bills regarding artificial limb implanted.
Atleast this fact is established that now with the help of artificial limb petitioner is pursuing her day to day affairs, functions including as an intern/student of BDS.

29. Hon'ble Apex Court in the matter of Raj Kumar vs. Ajay Kumar (supra) has laid down that Tribunal is bound to assess the evidence on the record, for the purpose of ascertaining the functional disability of the petitioner on account of medical permanent disability to assess how much the medical disability adversely affected on the functional capacity of the petitioner/injured so that just and fair amount of compensation can be ascertained under the heading of future loss of earning.

30. In the present case having noted the nature of the job of petitioner Neha being intern and the nature of the injury i.e. amputation of lower right MACT No.334/2017 Page 14 limb, this Tribunal taking into consideration the fact that petitioner has also implanted artificial limb but also taking note of the fact that job of the doctor/BDS is to move from one place to another to not only study BDS but also to work as intern and therefore on account of depriving of lower right leg limb, this Tribunal ascertain functional disability of petitioner to the extent of 45% vis a vis permanent medical disability of 60%.

Further, law is well settled that there should be no departure from the multiplier method in injury cases also [refer: Sandeep Khanuja vs. Atul Dande & Anr., (2017) 3 SCC 351].

As such at the time of accident petitioner was little more than 22 years of age.

As such multiplier to be applied in the present case would be 18 as applicable to age group between 21 to 25 years, would be applicable as per settled principle laid down in case of Sarla Verma v. DTC (2009) 6 SCC 121.

Moreover, the law has been well settled by the decisions of Supreme Court in the cases of Sandeep Khanuja (supra) and Erudhaya Priya vs.

Thus, considering the petitioner being below 25 years at the time of accident, in view of the judgment in Pranay Sethi & Others (supra) an addition of income to the extent of 40%
towards future prospects has to be counted.

32. As discussed above, the income of petitioner has been assessed as Rs.12,000/- + 40%
(Rs.4,800/-), total Rs.16,800/- (Rs.12,000 + Rs.4,800).
Thus applying the functional disability to be 45% of Rs.16,800/-, amount comes out to be Rs.7,560/-.
As such the loss of future income due to MACT No.334/2017 Page 15 disability comes out to be Rs.7560 X 12 X 18 = Rs.16,32,960/-.
Future Medical Expenses 33.

Petitioner/PW1 in her deposition has inter alia deposed that she would need a pair of artificial limb/prosthesis for rest of her life and has further stated that it would cost Rs.30 lakhs for maintenance of her artificial limb.

However in the entire evidence of PW1 as well as other witnesses,
there is no medical document/certificate issued from treating doctor to state that in future petitioner would require artificial limb for whole of her life.

This Tribunal is very much conscious of the fact that petitioner has lost lower right limb by amputation due to serious nature of injuries and had already implanted an artificial limb, for which compensation amount under medical expenses has already been given above.
But regarding the claim of the petitioner that Rs.30 lakhs would be spent for maintenance of artificial limb, no document has been proved on the record.
Although one certification from Ottobock regarding artificial limb future expenses has been placed on record.
But that document has not been proved even in the evidence of PW3 Dr.Shubham Bhardwaj, Prosthetist of Ottobock Health Care.

When the doctor/PW3 from Ottobock only proved the invoice of artificial limb Ex.PW3/B but has not proved the document as noted above regarding future maintenance of artificial limb to the tune of Rs.30 lakhs, in the absence of proof of that document this Tribunal cannot conclude regarding awarding of compensation for Rs.30 lakhs as claimed for future maintenance of artificial limb.
More particularly when even no medical prescription/certificate has been proved.

34. However this Tribunal taking into consideration the nature of injury, and the fact that petitioner has got implanted artificial limb, fix compensation of Rs.2,00,000/- on estimate basis under the heading of MACT No.334/2017 Page 16 future medical expenses.

Special Diet & Conveyance Charges:
Neha vs Anil Kumar on 17 November, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/126686646/
10 35.

Petitioner (PW1) in her evidence by way of affidavit deposed that an amount of Rs.4,00,000/-
has been incurred by her on transportation charges, special food, attendant charges and diet etc. till today and her condition is still not good as before accident.

Though petitioner has proved on record her medical treatment documents, but no documentary evidence in the form of prescription of doctor or bills of transportation and special diet has been placed on record to substantiate her claim that she has incurred expenses of Rs.4,00,000/- towards for transportation and special diet.

In the absence of any such documentary proof, this Tribunal while taking into consideration seriousness of injuries suffered by petitioner and the fact that her right lower limb has been amputated and artificial limb has been implanted, finds it appropriate to grant compensation for a sum of Rs.50,000/- towards conveyance charges and a sum of Rs.1,00,000/- towards special diet.

Attendant Charges:
36.
So far as charges under the head of attendant charges are concerned, petitioner has claimed compensation of Rs.4,00,000/- including attendant charges.
However no documentary proof in support thereof has been placed on record.
But fact remains that as noted in earlier part of the order, petitioner remained under medical treatment for five months till her discharge from the hospital lastly on 09.05.2017.
It has also come on record that right lower limb of the petitioner was amputated and an artificial limb has been planted.

In view of seriousness of injuries to petitioner,
period of her medical treatment as well as amputation and implantation of artificial limb, this Tribunal finds it appropriate if MACT No.334/2017 Page 17 compensation for a sum of Rs.50,000/-
is awarded under this head.

NON PECUNIARY DAMAGES :
Pain & Sufferings:
37.

While discussing the criteria to ascertain the compensation for pain and sufferings by victim of vehicular accident, observations of Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in Satya Narain v. Jai Kishan, FAO No:
709/02, date of decision: 02.02.2007 can be considered:
"12.
On account of pain and suffering, suffice would it be to note that it is difficult to measure pain and suffering in terms of a money value.
However, compensation which has to be paid must bear some objectives co-relation with the pain and suffering.

This means that the tribunal should consider and decide with reference to the evidence:
 (i) Whether the disablement is permanent or  temporary;
 (ii) If the disablement is permanent, whether it is permanent total disablement or permanent partial disablement;
(iii) If the disablement percentage is expressed with reference to any specific limb,
then the effect of such disablement of the limb on the functioning of the entire body,
that is the permanent disability suffered by the person.
If the Tribunal concludes that there is no permanent disability then there is no question of proceeding further and determining the loss of future earning capacity.
After the Tribunal ascertains the actual extent of permanent disability of the claimant based on the medical evidence, it has to determine whether such permanent disability has affected or will affect his earning capacity.
10. Ascertainment of the effect of the permanent disability on the actual earning capacity involves three steps.
The tribunal has to first ascertain what activities of the claimant could carry on in spite of the permanent disability and what he could not do as a result of permanent disability (this is also relevant for awarding compensation under the head of loss of amenities of life).
The third step is to find out whether (i) the claimant is totally disabled from earning any kind of livelihood or (ii) whether in spite of the permanent disability, the claimant could still effectively carry on the activities and functions, which he was earlier carrying on, or (iii) Whether he was prevented or restricted from discharging his previous activities and functions so that he continues to earn or MACT No.334/2017 Page 12 can continue to earn his livelihood."
....If doctor has given evidence about percentage of permanent disability, Tribunal will have to seek doctors opinion as to whether it is possible to deduce the corresponding functional permanent disability with reference to whole body and if so to what percentage.

Holistic view is to be taken while dealing with the Claim Petition based upon negligence.
Strict rules of evidence are not applicable in an inquiry conducted by the Claims Tribunal.
